findings.claim: High tariffs — the Fordney-McCumber Tariff of 1921 — protected American manufacturers from foreign competition. Repeated in the knowledge check ("Which tariff act of 1921..."), the flashcard ("the Fordney-McCumber Tariff (1921)") and the first practice mark scheme.
findings.truth: The Fordney-McCumber Tariff was signed by Harding in September 1922. The 1921 tariff was the separate Emergency Tariff Act. A student who writes 1921 for Fordney-McCumber gives a wrong date on a named act.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Fordney-McCumber Tariff' (signed September 1922; Emergency Tariff of 1921 listed as a separate earlier act)

findings.claim: Three Republican administrations — Harding (1921–23), Coolidge (1923–29), and Hoover (1929) — followed a broadly laissez-faire approach.
findings.truth: Hoover was president from 1929 to 1933. The bare '(1929)' reads as a one-year term and contradicts the lesson's own knowledge check, which matches Hoover to 1929–1933.
findings.evidence: internal inconsistency with knowledge_checks[4]; standard presidential dates

findings.claim: The Great Migration, in which hundreds of thousands of African Americans moved from the rural South to northern cities between roughly 1910 and 1930.
findings.truth: The accepted figure for 1910–1930 is about 1.6 million, which is what lesson 4 of this same unit states. 'Hundreds of thousands' understates it and conflicts with the sibling lesson.
findings.evidence: lesson 4 content_html of this unit; standard First Great Migration figure

findings.claim: Every lesson's six practice questions carry another board's question forms: '5 marks — Outline', '10 marks — Explain Two Reasons', '4 marks — Describe Two Features', '25 marks — Essay Using Interpretations (with SPaG)' and '15 marks — Compare Two Interpretations'. Two essay mark schemes also tell students to use interpretations and award 5 SPaG marks.
findings.truth: In this qualification the non-British depth study is worth 40 marks and is examined by four or five questions: 'Describe...' 2 marks, 'Explain...' 10 marks, then either one 10-mark source question or two 5-mark source questions (always two sources), and an 18-mark essay. There are no interpretation questions and no SPaG marks in this part of the paper — SPaG attaches only to question 4 of the period study on paper 1 and question 2 of the British depth study on paper 3. The 5-mark Outline, the 25-mark interpretations essay and the 25-mark interpretation comparison all belong to the period study, not here. There is no 4-mark 'Describe two features' form anywhere in the qualification. Relabelled all 54 questions: two 2-mark Describes, two 10-mark Explains, one 18-mark Essay, one 10-mark Source Comparison per lesson, with mark schemes rebuilt to match.
findings.evidence: spec assessment tables for component group 1 (both depth-study variants) and section 3i on spelling, punctuation and grammar

findings.claim: ...the Great Migration as an economic response — examiners reward students who show multiple strategies.
findings.truth: An invented claim about examiner behaviour. No published examiner statement supports it. Reworded as advice in the site's own voice.
findings.evidence: no source; house rule against fabricated examiner claims

findings.claim: On the NAACP vs. UNIA distinction, examiners reward answers that can explain the different strategies...
findings.truth: Invented examiner claim. Reworded as direct advice.
findings.evidence: no source; house rule against fabricated examiner claims

findings.claim: This is inaccurate, and examiners penalise oversimplification. (content_html) and 'Examiners consistently report that students describe Hoover as doing "nothing" about the Depression.' (exam_tip_html)
findings.truth: Both are invented claims about examiner reports and examiner behaviour. The underlying teaching point — that 'Hoover did nothing' is wrong and loses marks — is kept, without attributing it to examiners.
findings.evidence: no source; house rule against fabricated examiner claims

findings.claim: This lesson has several specific facts that examiners test directly... Examiners reward students who can discuss both the limits and the significance of wartime changes.
findings.truth: Two invented examiner claims in one tip. Reworded as advice in the site's own voice.
findings.evidence: no source; house rule against fabricated examiner claims

findings.claim: Garvey was convicted of mail fraud in 1925 and deported to Jamaica in 1927, ending his American movement. Repeated in the flashcard 'What happened to Marcus Garvey in 1925-27?'
findings.truth: Garvey was convicted of mail fraud on 18 June 1923. He stayed free on bail during appeals, began his sentence in Atlanta in 1925, and was deported to Jamaica in 1927 after Coolidge commuted the sentence. 1925 is the year he was jailed, not convicted.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Marcus Garvey' (jury verdict 18 June 1923; imprisoned 1925–1927; deported 1927)

findings.claim: In April 1920, two Italian-born anarchists, Nicola Sacco and Bartolomeo Vanzetti, were arrested for the murder of a paymaster and his guard during a robbery in South Braintree, Massachusetts.
findings.truth: The South Braintree robbery and murders were on 15 April 1920. Sacco and Vanzetti were arrested on 5 May 1920. The lesson gives the crime date as the arrest date.
findings.evidence: standard case chronology (robbery 15 April 1920, arrests 5 May 1920, trial 1921, execution 23 August 1927)

findings.claim: The spec for this lesson also requires knowledge of attempts to combat prejudice.
findings.truth: Pipeline meta-commentary left in student-facing prose. The content point is correct — the specification does list attempts to combat prejudice — but a student reading the article should not be told what the build brief required. Replaced with a plain topic sentence.
findings.evidence: spec content list for this depth study ('attempts to combat prejudice, including the NAACP and the UNIA')

findings.claim: Present their case as procedurally flawed rather than asserting innocence as established fact.
findings.truth: An instruction written for the content author, left inside the article. The judgement it carries is right and is already made in the exam tip. Reworded as a statement to the student.
findings.evidence: internal: same point already made in exam_tip_html

findings.claim: The 2001 Oklahoma Commission... concluded that at least 36 people died. Repeated in the flashcard and in the third practice mark scheme.
findings.truth: 36 is the figure officially recorded by the Oklahoma Bureau of Vital Statistics. The 2001 Commission confirmed 39 dead (26 Black, 13 white) from death certificates and autopsy reports, and reported estimates running up to about 300. The lesson attaches the wrong number to the Commission.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Tulsa race massacre' (Bureau of Vital Statistics 36; 2001 Commission identified 39; estimates to c.300; more than 35 blocks destroyed)

findings.claim: Unemployment rose from around 3 per cent in 1929 to a peak of approximately 25 per cent by 1932 — around 13 to 15 million people out of work. The exam tip repeats 'peak unemployment was around 1932'.
findings.truth: Unemployment peaked in 1933 at about 24.9 per cent; 1932 was about 23.6 per cent. The peak number out of work was about 13 million, not 15 million. Dating the peak to 1932 also misleads about sequence, because the worst point came at Roosevelt's inauguration in March 1933.
findings.evidence: standard Lebergott/BLS annual unemployment series (1932 23.6%, 1933 24.9%)

findings.claim: His 'Share Our Wealth' plan proposed to cap personal fortunes at $3 million. Repeated in the flashcard and in two practice mark schemes.
findings.truth: Long proposed limiting an individual's private fortune to $50 million, with his tax structure capping fortunes at $100 million. $3 million is not one of his figures. The $2,000 minimum family income in the lesson is right (his plan promised $2,000–3,000 plus a $5,000 household estate).
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Share Our Wealth' (cap of $100 million; private wealth limit of $50 million; household estate $5,000; minimum income $2,000–3,000; 7.5 million members in 27,000 clubs by 1935)

findings.claim: Their record of never losing a bomber to enemy fighters became a source of immense pride.
findings.truth: The 'never lost a bomber' claim is a wartime press story that later research disproved: the Air Force Historical Research Agency study of 2007 identified at least 27 bombers lost to enemy fighters while under 332nd Fighter Group escort. The Tuskegee Airmen's record was outstanding, but this specific claim is not true and should not be taught as fact.
findings.evidence: Air Force Historical Research Agency study (2007) as reported in Wikipedia, 'Tuskegee Airmen'

findings.claim: The sixth practice question in every lesson was an interpretation comparison with the two interpretations summarised inside the question stem. It is now relabelled as the 10-mark source comparison, with the two positions given as 'Source A says... Source B says...' rather than as printed sources.
findings.truth: Two defensible readings. (a) Leave as is: the form, the marks and the two-source rule are now correct, no provenance is invented, and the item drills the comparison skill. (b) Commission two short real extracts per lesson (a contemporary newspaper line, a speech, a photograph caption) so students practise using provenance as well as content, which the real question rewards. Option (b) is better preparation but is a 9-lesson authoring job with a licensing check on each extract. My recommendation is (a) now and (b) as a separate queued piece of work, because the mark-affecting error (the label) is fixed either way and inventing provenance to fill the gap would be worse than leaving the extracts out.
findings.evidence: spec assessment table for the depth study, question 7 ('learners will always have two sources to deal with')
findings.ruling: Leave: paraphrased views stand until genuine extracts are authored (source-bank rebuild).

findings.claim: By 1929, US car production had reached approximately 5.6 million vehicles a year. Repeated in a flashcard and a practice mark scheme.
findings.truth: US factory sales in 1929 are usually given as about 5.34 million motor vehicles, of which about 4.46 million were passenger cars. 5.6 million is roughly five per cent high. I could not confirm a true value from the sources allowed in this pass, so no edit is written.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Automotive industry in the United States' gives no 1929 figure; standard series is 5,337,087 vehicles

findings.claim: The iconic cultural figure of Rosie the Riveter, with the slogan 'We Can Do It!'
findings.truth: The 'We Can Do It!' poster was made for Westinghouse in 1943 by J. Howard Miller and had no connection with Rosie the Riveter at the time; the two were only merged in popular memory from the 1980s. The conflation is universal in GCSE textbooks and costs no marks, so it is recorded rather than edited.
findings.evidence: standard poster history

findings.claim: the CIO (Congress of Industrial Organisations), a new federation for industrial workers, grew rapidly — in a passage about 1935.
findings.truth: In 1935 the body was the Committee for Industrial Organization, a group inside the AFL. It became the Congress of Industrial Organizations in 1938. A mild anachronism that does not affect an answer about the Wagner Act.
findings.evidence: standard CIO chronology

summary: Nine lessons checked against the board specification. The dominant error is unit-wide: every practice question in all nine lessons carried another board's question forms, including a 4-mark 'Describe two features', a 25-mark interpretations essay with 5 SPaG marks and a 15-mark interpretation comparison, none of which exist in this depth study — all 54 questions relabelled to the real forms (Describe 2, Explain 10, Source Comparison 10, Essay 18, no SPaG, no interpretations). On top of that, six factual errors: the Fordney-McCumber Tariff dated 1921 not 1922, Garvey convicted in 1925 not 1923, Huey Long's wealth cap given as $3 million not $50 million, Sacco and Vanzetti arrested in April not May 1920, the Tulsa death toll misattributed to the 2001 Commission, and the Tuskegee Airmen's disproved 'never lost a bomber' claim taught as fact; plus five invented examiner claims across four exam tips. 143 edits.
